experiment_design.technical_details: This study designs a computational saturation analysis to test the hypothesis that cancer molecular heterogeneity is non-asymptotic. Using TCGA pan-cancer data, we will quantify the rate of novel driver mutation combination discovery as a function of sample size (N). The core technical challenge is defining 'unique driver combinations' robustly. We will use established oncogenic driver lists (e.g., OncoKB or COSMIC consensus) to filter somatic variants from TCGA WES/WGS data. We will then construct a 'mutation signature space' where each tumor is represented by a binary vector of present/absent driver genes. The primary metric is the 'Novelty Discovery Rate' (NDR), defined as the number of unique binary vectors found in the Nth sample that were not present in the previous N-1 samples. We will fit power-law and logarithmic models to the cumulative count of unique signatures vs. N. If the best-fit model is linear or super-linear (power law exponent >= 1), it supports the hypothesis of infinite heterogeneity. If it saturates (logarithmic or asymptotic), it suggests a finite target space. We will also perform pathway-level convergence analysis to test if genetic heterogeneity maps to a finite set of functional states.

experiment_design.methods: 1. Data Preprocessing: Download TCGA somatic mutation MAF files for all available cancer types. Filter for high-confidence somatic mutations using standard quality flags. Map mutations to genes and annotate with driver status using curated driver gene lists. 2. Signature Construction: For each tumor sample, create a binary vector representing the presence/absence of mutations in known driver genes. Optionally, include co-mutation patterns (pairs/triples) to capture combinatorial complexity. 3. Saturation Analysis: Randomly subsample the dataset from N=100 to N=max (total samples) in increments. For each N, calculate the cumulative number of unique mutation signatures observed. Plot Unique Signatures vs. N. 4. Model Fitting: Fit three models to the curve: (a) Linear (infinite growth), (b) Power Law (slow infinite growth), (c) Logarithmic/Asymptotic (finite space). Use AIC/BIC for model selection. 5. Pathway Convergence Test: Map mutations to KEGG/Reactome pathways. Calculate pathway activity scores (e.g., via ssGSEA) for each sample. Cluster samples based on pathway activity and determine if the number of distinct clusters saturates as N increases.

baselines: Random Mutation Model: Simulate mutations distributed randomly across genes to establish a null hypothesis for diversity growth.
Pan-Cancer Agnostic Baseline: Assume all tumors are identical (single signature) to demonstrate the lower bound of heterogeneity.
Single-Cancer Type Baseline: Perform saturation analysis within homogeneous cancer types (e.g., Lung Adenocarcinoma only) to contrast with pan-cancer heterogeneity.
metrics: Novelty Discovery Rate (NDR): The slope of new unique signatures per added sample.
Goodness-of-Fit (R-squared/AIC): For linear vs. asymptotic models describing signature accumulation.
Coverage Ratio: The percentage of total samples covered by the top-K most frequent mutation signatures.
ablation: Driver Definition Sensitivity: Vary the stringency of 'driver' definition (strict consensus vs. broad candidate list) to test robustness.
Co-mutation Depth: Analyze single-gene mutations vs. pairwise vs. triple-wise combinations to see if combinatorial explosion drives the non-asymptotic trend.
Tissue Type Stratification: Exclude rare cancer types to ensure results are not driven by outlier histologies.
experiments.validation_protocol: Split TCGA data into 80% training (for model fitting) and 20% hold-out test set. Verify if the fitted saturation model predicts the number of new signatures in the hold-out set accurately. Cross-validate across different cancer types to ensure generalizability.

experiment_design.technical_details: This study designs a computational saturation analysis to test the hypothesis that cancer molecular heterogeneity is non-asymptotic. Using TCGA pan-cancer data, we will quantify the rate of novel driver mutation combination discovery as a function of sample size (N). The core technical challenge is defining 'unique driver combinations' robustly. We will use established oncogenic driver lists (e.g., OncoKB or COSMIC consensus) to filter somatic variants from TCGA WES/WGS data. We will then construct a 'mutation signature space' where each tumor is represented by a binary vector of present/absent driver genes. The primary metric is the 'Novelty Discovery Rate' (NDR), defined as the number of unique binary vectors found in the Nth sample that were not present in the previous N-1 samples. We will fit power-law and logarithmic models to the cumulative count of unique signatures vs. N. If the best-fit model is linear or super-linear (power law exponent >= 1), it supports the hypothesis of infinite heterogeneity. If it saturates (logarithmic or asymptotic), it suggests a finite target space. We will also perform pathway-level convergence analysis to test if genetic heterogeneity maps to a finite set of functional states.

experiment_design.methods: 1. Data Preprocessing: Download TCGA somatic mutation MAF files for all available cancer types. Filter for high-confidence somatic mutations using standard quality flags. Map mutations to genes and annotate with driver status using curated driver gene lists. 2. Signature Construction: For each tumor sample, create a binary vector representing the presence/absence of mutations in known driver genes. Optionally, include co-mutation patterns (pairs/triples) to capture combinatorial complexity. 3. Saturation Analysis: Randomly subsample the dataset from N=100 to N=max (total samples) in increments. For each N, calculate the cumulative number of unique mutation signatures observed. Plot Unique Signatures vs. N. 4. Model Fitting: Fit three models to the curve: (a) Linear (infinite growth), (b) Power Law (slow infinite growth), (c) Logarithmic/Asymptotic (finite space). Use AIC/BIC for model selection. 5. Pathway Convergence Test: Map mutations to KEGG/Reactome pathways. Calculate pathway activity scores (e.g., via ssGSEA) for each sample. Cluster samples based on pathway activity and determine if the number of distinct clusters saturates as N increases.

baselines: Random Mutation Model: Simulate mutations distributed randomly across genes to establish a null hypothesis for diversity growth.
Pan-Cancer Agnostic Baseline: Assume all tumors are identical (single signature) to demonstrate the lower bound of heterogeneity.
Single-Cancer Type Baseline: Perform saturation analysis within homogeneous cancer types (e.g., Lung Adenocarcinoma only) to contrast with pan-cancer heterogeneity.
metrics: Novelty Discovery Rate (NDR): The slope of new unique signatures per added sample.
Goodness-of-Fit (R-squared/AIC): For linear vs. asymptotic models describing signature accumulation.
Coverage Ratio: The percentage of total samples covered by the top-K most frequent mutation signatures.
ablation: Driver Definition Sensitivity: Vary the stringency of 'driver' definition (strict consensus vs. broad candidate list) to test robustness.
Co-mutation Depth: Analyze single-gene mutations vs. pairwise vs. triple-wise combinations to see if combinatorial explosion drives the non-asymptotic trend.
Tissue Type Stratification: Exclude rare cancer types to ensure results are not driven by outlier histologies.
experiments.validation_protocol: Split TCGA data into 80% training (for model fitting) and 20% hold-out test set. Verify if the fitted saturation model predicts the number of new signatures in the hold-out set accurately. Cross-validate across different cancer types to ensure generalizability.

experiment_design.technical_details: This study designs a computational saturation analysis to test the hypothesis that cancer molecular heterogeneity is non-asymptotic. Using TCGA pan-cancer data, we will quantify the rate of novel driver mutation combination discovery as a function of sample size (N). The core technical challenge is defining 'unique driver combinations' robustly. We will use established oncogenic driver lists (e.g., OncoKB or COSMIC consensus) to filter somatic variants from TCGA WES/WGS data. We will then construct a 'mutation signature space' where each tumor is represented by a binary vector of present/absent driver genes. The primary metric is the 'Novelty Discovery Rate' (NDR), defined as the number of unique binary vectors found in the Nth sample that were not present in the previous N-1 samples. We will fit power-law and logarithmic models to the cumulative count of unique signatures vs. N. If the best-fit model is linear or super-linear (power law exponent >= 1), it supports the hypothesis of infinite heterogeneity. If it saturates (logarithmic or asymptotic), it suggests a finite target space. We will also perform pathway-level convergence analysis to test if genetic heterogeneity maps to a finite set of functional states.

Pathway Convergence Test: Map mutations to KEGG/Reactome pathways. Calculate pathway activity scores (e.g., via ssGSEA) for each sample. Cluster samples based on pathway activity and determine if the number of distinct clusters saturates as N increases.
